title: Navigating the MAD MAP: Mutual Assured Destruction vs. Mutual Assured Prosperity
synopsis: Presents two possible AI futures: Mutual Assured Destruction through conflict and fragmentation, or Mutual Assured Prosperity through cooperation.

content:
I've been thinking about maps lately. I mean the mental models we use to navigate an uncertain future rather than the geographical kind. The maps we choose to follow determine, to a remarkable degree, the destinations we reach.

With artificial intelligence I see two fundamentally different maps being drawn. Both describe the same territory and they lead to very different places. I've taken to calling them MAD and MAP - Mutual Assured Destruction and Mutual Assured Prosperity.

The technology itself is agnostic. Artificial intelligence is an amplifier, making possible things that were previously impossible without determining what those things will be. That choice remains, for now, in human hands, and the only question is what we choose to amplify.

**The First Map**

The MAD map isn't difficult to describe. In this future, AI becomes an accelerant for human conflict and fragmentation. Autonomous weapons operate at machine speed, too fast for human judgement to intervene. Cyber attacks grow more sophisticated and more frequent. Disinformation becomes the ambient background noise of public discourse. Trust in institutions erodes to the point where collective action becomes impossible.

Consider what machine-speed warfare actually involves. Human reaction time operates in hundreds of milliseconds and these systems operate in fractions of that. A conflict between autonomous systems would unfold faster than any person could comprehend, let alone control, with escalation occurring in the space between one breath and the next. The pause that has historically prevented catastrophe - the moment when a decision-maker hesitates, reconsiders, chooses de-escalation - disappears entirely. We would have built systems capable of ending civilisation and removed our own capacity to stop them.

The disinformation problem may prove equally corrosive and considerably less dramatic. We're approaching a threshold where generating convincing falsehood becomes cheaper than verifying truth. Every image can be fabricated, every video synthesised, every voice cloned. When the cost of producing a lie approaches zero and the cost of debunking one stays substantial, the economics favour deception. Truth becomes exhausting rather than impossible - a luxury requiring resources most people don't have.

What follows is the collapse of shared reality, and we've already seen the early stages: people inhabiting different factual universes, unable to agree on what happened let alone what should be done. AI accelerates the fragmentation, because when anyone can generate evidence for any claim, evidence itself becomes suspect. The common ground required for collective action erodes and we become a society of isolated individuals, each in a personalised information environment, unable to coordinate even where coordination is obviously in everyone's interest.

That's what trust erosion looks like in practice. A slow acidification rather than a dramatic betrayal. Institutions lose legitimacy through accumulated doubt rather than single failures - each small deception, each manipulation revealed, each synthetic media incident adding to the corrosion, until the structures enabling cooperation become too weak to bear weight. By the time anyone notices, rebuilding may take generations.

What makes this scenario insidious is that it never arrives through catastrophe. It unfolds gradually, one small erosion at a time, and each individual step seems manageable. A slightly more capable weapon system. A somewhat more convincing deepfake. A marginally more polarised discourse. No single development crosses a bright line, and it's only when you look up that you see how far you've drifted from shore.

That's the nature of drift. The current carries you so gently that movement is imperceptible. You adjust to each new position and treat it as the baseline from which to measure future change. The shore that once seemed close becomes distant, then faint, then invisible, and at no point can you identify the moment when return became impossible, because there was no such moment. There was only the accumulation of small movements, each insignificant, together constituting a journey you never chose.

**The Second Map**

The MAP alternative imagines something else entirely. Here artificial intelligence becomes the most powerful problem-solving tool humanity has ever held. Disease yields to accelerated drug discovery. Poverty retreats before optimised resource distribution. Education becomes personalised in ways that unlock human potential at scale. The rate at which we generate solutions begins to exceed the rate at which new problems emerge.

I want to be clear that MAP describes something short of utopia. Problems don't disappear; they become more manageable. What changes is the ratio between our capacity to address challenges and the severity of the challenges themselves.

Both maps describe futures that are physically possible. The question is which one we navigate towards, and the decisions of the next few years will settle it.

Some concern how we regulate. Governance moving at the speed of the technology, rather than years behind it, can integrate safety without sacrificing innovation, while delay guarantees that the most dangerous applications reach deployment before oversight catches up.

But what would governance at technological speed actually look like? Our institutions were designed for a world where change happened slowly enough to study and deliberate and respond. Legislation takes years and regulatory frameworks take longer, and by the time oversight reaches a technology that technology has transformed and been replaced. We're attempting to regulate with tools built for a different temporal reality.

Perhaps it requires entirely new mechanisms. Regulatory sandboxes permitting experimentation inside boundaries. AI systems monitoring AI systems, providing oversight at the speed of the thing overseen. International coordination structures that respond in weeks rather than decades. I don't know whether any of these are achievable. I do know that governing exponential change with linear institutions is a recipe for permanent lag.

Other decisions concern work. These systems will automate tasks before they automate jobs, and the destination is a fundamental restructuring of how human beings contribute economically. That's an opportunity to create new forms of meaningful work, available only if we invest seriously in adaptation instead of offering platitudes about reskilling.

Privacy presents another fork. These systems process unprecedented quantities of personal information, and without data ownership and consent built into the architecture from the beginning we drift towards surveillance as the default. Retrofitting privacy afterwards will prove extraordinarily difficult.

Most importantly, we have to decide whether to treat AI development as a zero-sum competition or an opportunity for cooperation. If nations treat it as a race to be won at any cost, MAD becomes close to inevitable. If we share safety research, develop interoperable standards, and cooperate on oversight of the most powerful systems, the probability of MAP rises substantially.

**Why the Precedents Worked**

I don't believe the future is predetermined. I believe it's shaped by an accumulation of choices, most of them small and many made without full awareness of their consequences. I also believe some moments matter more than others, and we're living through one now.

Humanity has navigated existential risk before. The Cuban Missile Crisis brought us to the brink and we stepped back. The Montreal Protocol addressed ozone depletion before it became irreversible. The Cold War ended without the conflagration that seemed inevitable for decades. None of those were accidents. They were choices, made by people and institutions that understood the stakes and acted.

What made them work? In each case there was sufficient shared understanding of the risk - the decision-makers grasped viscerally what failure would mean. And there was time. Time to recognise the danger, to communicate, to negotiate, to choose differently.

I'm not certain we'll have that time here. The technology moves faster than nuclear proliferation or atmospheric chemistry. The feedback loops are shorter. The decision points may arrive and pass before anyone recognises them as decision points, which is a reason for urgency rather than despair.

If I had to name the single mechanism most worth building now, it would be a standing international channel between the frontier labs and their counterparts in rival states - technical, continuous, and insulated from the diplomatic weather. A treaty takes a decade. I mean the equivalent of the hotline that came out of the Cuban Missile Crisis.

I'd argue for that first because every precedent I listed required communication to already exist before it was needed. The hotline wasn't built during the crisis. It was built afterwards, by people who'd just discovered they had no way to talk to each other at the moment it mattered most. We currently have no such channel for this technology, and we're proposing to find out whether we need one the same way they did.

We have the capacity to navigate towards MAP. Capacity isn't certainty, and the window for action isn't unlimited. The current carries us whether we paddle or not, and the only real question is whether we steer.
